The Light of the Revival Stained Glass Exhibition Debuts in Walsh Library Adithi Vimalanathan , Contribu

  Eugeny Kotylar is a professor of art history at the Kharkiv State Academy of Design and Arts in Kharkiv, Ukraine, and came to Fordham through the AAJR-Fordham-NYPL Fellowship for Ukrainian Scholars . He first began working with stained glass in the 1990s amidst a cultural and community movement in Ukraine to restore houses of worship that were desecrated and often destroyed by years of Soviet rule. “Many of the sacred buildings, churches, synagogues were appropriated for swimming pools, for storage facilities, or if they were lucky, for archives for workers clubs… As a result, many of the synagogues were either destroyed or certainly the sacred art has been destroyed,” said Professor Magda Teter, chair of Shvidler Studies at Fordham and administrator of the fellowship program Kotlyar completed. Jewish architecture, including existing stained glass windows, were lost to pogroms such as Kristallnacht, where Nazis burned over 900 synagogues in a single night. 

  Kotlyar began creating these stained glass windows in 1993 for a course project while a student at the Kharkiv Art and Industrial Institute. The first of his designs was for the Kharkiv Choral Synagogue, the largest in the country. In his opening remarks at the exhibition, Kotlyar described his moment of inspiration: “When inside, I raised my head up to where the dome was rising, and seeing the crumbling plaster, I said to myself, ‘Oh, I would create something like the Sistine Chapel by the great Michelangelo here.’” He designed two windows on the theme of Jewish holidays which would have run along the sides of the synagogue. The final result was unfortunately never implemented as it was lost to a fire, but his original designs and images are currently on display in Walsh Library. The exhibit features two additional designs by Kotlyar, one for a synagogue in Podil and another for one in Kyiv.

Stained glass - Designing Buildings

  We use cookies to ensure we give you the best experience on our website.

 Stained glass  Stained glass is a type of glazing material that is coloured ( stained ), either by the addition of metallic salts during the manufacturing process , or by having colour applied to its surface and then being fired in a kiln to fuse the colour to the glass . 

   Stained glass can be used for a wide range of purposes, but it is most commonly found in flat panels in windows .  Stained glass windows typically comprise small pieces of coloured glass held in place by a latticed web of lead strips formed within a rigid frame . The pieces are often arranged to create patterns or pictorial representations, often depicting religious iconography. 

   Stained glass windows are commonly associated with cathedrals , churches, mosques and other important buildings such as libraries and town halls . In England , the use of simple  stained glass windows dates back to the 7th century, and by the 12th century they had become a sophisticated art form . However, following the Reformation in the 16th century, when sacred art began to decline in prominence, the craft of manufacturing  stained glass began to dwindle. 

  Historic England 2020 Stained Glass Windows: Managing Environmental Deterioration , Swindon, Historic England , published in 2020 states: ‘ Stained glass is not the only means of producing a decorative window ; others include etching, engraving or ‘ fritting ’. One of the most important alternative methods is dalle-de-verre , where thick pieces of glass are set directly into a matrix of resin or concrete . This technique was used to form some of the most dramatic and important  stained glass in the periods before and immediately after World War II, but as with all innovative systems , it can sometimes present serious conservation challenges. More tricky still to preserve are windows incorporating fibreglass , or even plastic.’

West Vancouver Memorial Library The West Vancouver Memorial Library, located at 1950 Marine Drive, was constructed in 1950, and opened to the public on November 11. The land on which it was built was donated by the District, but the building itself was paid for through public subscription. Previous to this construction, there were a number of small lending libraries scattered through West Vancouver, including one run by Ambleside shopkeeper, Mrs. Effie M. Field. As well, some books were available through the Provincial government's 'travelling libraries.' In 1921, the Hollyburn Public Library Association was formed, and with it, a public voice concerned with building a library. After World War II, it was decided to build a library as a memorial to honour local fallen soldiers. Since the original opening in 1950, there have been four additions, in 1957, 1962 (when the Jubilee wing was built), 1977 (when 1,400 square meters of space was added) and 1993. In 1996, the West Vancouver Memorial Library won an award as being the 'Best Library in Canada.' Today, the library is an invaluable resource for the community. Art pieces at the library include the hand-finished, composite alabaster 'Discus Thower,' two untitled paintings by E.H. Statement of Significance War Memorial Memorial Gardens Park West Vancouver, BC April 2008 2

Historic Place 

The historic place is the War Memorial, a stone arch, along with the adjacent Cairn, Plinths, and landscaped ground in Memorial Park on Marine Drive and 19 th Street in West Vancouver. Together with the West Vancouver Memorial Library, located across the street (and not a part of the historic place), the two sites form a memorial precinct commemorating those West Vancouverites who fell in several wars. The library houses a memorial stained glass window and an official book for remembrance. 

Heritage Value 

The War Memorial has considerable value to the community as the place where West Vancouver residents have gathered every Remembrance Day since its dedication in 1925, to remember those who have fallen in the wars. It is one of the earliest formal celebration places in the community. The Cairn remembers the 21 residents who fell in World War I, while the two Plinths remember the fallen from World War II. Over the years, the War Memorial has grown into an ecumenical spiritual gathering place. The War Memorial also has value as a sculpted arch, with its rusticated stonework and interesting detail. The Cairn is an appropriate adjunct, with a tablet bearing names framed by a rusticated monument. Memorial Park has value as a secluded landscaped area for remembrance and contemplation.

In 1919 Effie Field set up a small lending library in her dry goods and children's clothing store at 14th Street and Bellevue Avenue. This became the Hollyburn Public Library Association in May 1921 and continued to operate out of her store. By 1926 the library had 1,000 books and moved from Mrs Field's store to George Gemmill's drug store at 1402 Marine Drive. The library moved again in 1929 to the Yates building west of the Ambleside Service Station. The Hollyburn Public Library closed in 1936, but a number of small lending libraries were established in the 1930s. Plans began in 1944 for a new library as a tribute to fallen soldiers in World War II.

Synopsis In 1919 Effie Field set up a small lending library in her dry goods and children's clothing store at 14th Street and Bellevue Avenue. This became the Hollyburn Public Library Association in May 1921 and continued to operate out of her store. By 1926 the library had 1,000 books and moved from Mrs Field's store to George Gemmill's drug store at 1402 Marine Drive. The library moved again in 1929 to the Yates building west of the Ambleside Service Station. The Hollyburn Public Library closed in 1936, but a number of small lending libraries were established in the 1930s. Plans began in 1944 for a new library as a tribute to fallen soldiers in World War II. Land was cleared by volunteer labour, and the architect and contractor waived their fees. Opened November 11, 1950 at 1950 Marine Drive, the West Vancouver Memorial Library was financed by subscribers, with two thousand dollars contributed by the Municipal Council. It was handed to the Municipal Council debt free. The architectural plans were donated by R.A.D. Berwick, and the memorial window presented by Mrs Allan S. Gentles in memory of her brother Lieut.
